clips.text: Welcome. This lesson follows the website, not the order of an audiobook. We will explore the heart as a pump, trace its electrical signal, zoom into muscle contraction, and connect the lungs to circulation. Then we will use those ideas to understand E C G recordings. Each short section has a matching transcript. Pause, replay, or explore before continuing. The later rhythm and pacemaker chapters are separate study modules.

clips.text: Begin with the whole system. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together in systems. Homeostasis means maintaining a relatively stable internal environment. The lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the air. The heart creates pressure that moves blood. Blood vessels distribute that blood, and tissues exchange gases and nutrients across capillaries. Oxygen delivery depends on all of these parts, not on one monitor number alone.

clips.text: Before we name a structure, establish the patient's directions. Right and left always mean the patient's right and left. Anterior means toward the front; posterior, toward the back. Superior means toward the head; inferior, toward the feet. Medial is toward the midline; lateral is away from it. A frontal plane separates front from back. A transverse plane separates upper from lower regions. A sagittal plane separates left from right.

clips.text: Locate the heart behind the sternum, between the lungs, in the mediastinum. Its apex points down and toward the patient's left. The adult heart is roughly the size of that person's fist, but size varies. The rib cage normally has twelve pairs of ribs. The spaces between adjacent ribs are intercostal spaces. These chest landmarks will matter again when we place recording electrodes.

clips.text: Add four pairs of location words. Proximal means closer to a point of attachment; distal means farther from it. The wrist is distal to the elbow. Superficial means nearer the body surface; deep means farther inside. Cranial and caudal roughly indicate toward the head and toward the lower end of the trunk. Ventral and dorsal usually correspond to anterior and posterior in the human trunk. Apply each term to a named structure rather than memorizing an isolated definition.

clips.text: Check your orientation. In a front view of the patient, is the patient's right side on your right or your left? Pause and point to it. Then identify the sternum and the space occupied by the heart. Continue when you can explain why patient-centered directions prevent mistakes when locating chest electrodes.
